To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
non-consciously retained visual information can be decoded from the neural activity in the occipital cortex and the activity in the frontal cortex can be used to predict memory performance.
non-consciously presented visual information is retained for up to 15 seconds, as shown by chance performance in a delayed match to sample task.
we used continuous flash-suppression to render stimuli non-consciously, and that we used fMRI to investigate short-term memory processes in the human brain.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question whether non-conscious stimuli are stored in a working memory buffer and if so how this is reflected in neural activity.
the neural mechanisms underlying non-conscious perception and memory.
the neural correlates of short-term retention of non-conscious information.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
non-conscious working memory relies on neural activity in frontal cortex and occipital regions, and is accompanied by increased BOLD signal in prefrontal cortex during memory recognition.
non-conscious information is retained for a limited period of time in a neural system that is very similar, if not identical, to that involved in the conscious maintenance of information.

the non-consciously perceived stimulus is retained for a short period of time, which is sufficient to be used for memory recognition, and that this retention is accompanied by neural activity patterns in frontal and occiptal cortex.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we found that the brain processes that underlie working memory can be used to maintain information that is not consciously perceived.
non-conscious working memory is a real and robust phenomenon.
the non-conscious visual working memory system is not only a memory buffer for the information that has been consciously attended, but also for information that was never consciously perceived.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the neural mechanisms of non-conscious working memory seem to be similar to those of conscious working memory, but with less capacity and less control over the information.
the brain is not a passive observer of the outside world, but actively processes the information it receives.

non-conscious short-term memory can be studied with the same methods as conscious memory, and that it can be investigated with the same methods used to investigate conscious perception, such as multivariate pattern analysis.
